44-125.r: Separate electorates for Muslims (to turn them against Congress) → Lord Minto (Viceroy from Nov 1905) with John Morley; Morley-Minto Reforms, Government of India Act 1909.

44-126.r: Only Jewish Viceroy of India → Lord Reading (Rufus Isaacs), 1921-1926; earlier Lord Chief Justice of England (1913).

44-127.r: Wrong pair: Vernacular Press Act ('Gagging Act') - Curzon → it was Lytton (1878). Correct: Pitt's India Act - Warren Hastings; Doctrine of Lapse - Dalhousie; Ilbert Bill - Ripon.

44-129.r: Capital moved from Calcutta to Delhi → Lord Hardinge II; announced at the third Delhi Durbar, 1911 (George V and Queen Mary), which also annulled the Partition of Bengal.

44-130.r: Doctrine of Lapse → Dalhousie; Partition of Bengal → Curzon; Dual Government in Bengal → Clive; Social Reforms → Bentinck.

44-131.r: GG of Bengal (1773 Act) → Cornwallis (Hastings not listed); GG of India (1833 Act) → Dalhousie; GG and Viceroy (1858) → Minto; GG and Crown Representative (1935) → Wavell.

44-132.r: Year of annexation: Satara → 1848; Sambalpur → 1849; Jhansi → 1854; Awadh → 1856.

44-133.r: Merger order: Sikkim part (Darjeeling) ceded 1835 → Punjab 1849 → Jhansi 1854 → Burma 1886. Sikkim never fully merged.
44-133.c: Answer not printed; explanation's dates give I, III, II, IV = option (d).

44-134.r: Titles 'Rai Bahadur' and 'Khan Bahadur' → first given to loyal rulers and zamindars for help in crushing the 1857 revolt (1859, 1860); none of the listed Viceroys.

45-001.r: Home Charges → India Office in London, salaries and pensions of British personnel, military stores, interest on debts and railway capital; not wars outside India.

45-002.r: 'Imperial preference' → special privileges for British imports in India (nominal duty), while Indian exports paid high duty in Britain.

45-003.r: No independent industrial growth under British rule → the rich preferred to invest in land.

45-004.r: EIC's staple exports from Bengal, mid-18th century → cotton (cloth), silk, saltpetre and opium (also sugar).

45-005.r: Istimrari (Permanent) Settlement, 1793 → Lord Cornwallis; made with landlords as owners; Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, Varanasi.

45-013.r: Permanent Settlement 1793: many zamindars issued no pattas because there was no official check on them; they only paid 10/11th of collections to government.

45-014.r: Permanent Settlement in Bihar → land revenue permanently fixed ('constitutionalised'), giving the Company a fixed income.

45-015.r: Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 → defined tenants' and landlords' rights in Bengal and Bihar after peasant revolts against rent hikes.

45-016.r: Ryotwari Settlement → Alexander Read and Thomas Munro, not Cornwallis; first in Baramahal district, Madras Presidency (acquired 1792); demand fixed at 50% of estimated produce.

45-018.r: Permanent Settlement → Bengal (also Bihar, Odisha, Varanasi); Ryotwari → Madras (also parts of Bombay, Assam, Coorg).

45-019.r: Thomas Munro → Ryotwari Settlement (with Captain Alexander Read); first in Baramahal (Tamil Nadu), then Madras, Assam, Coorg, parts of Bombay; ownership to peasants.
45-019.h: Munro → Madras → Ryotwari: three Rs/Ms of the south.

45-024.r: Ryotwari first introduced → Madras Presidency; devised by Alexander Read and Thomas Munro, brought in by Munro as Governor of Madras.

45-025.r: Ryotwari: peasants paid rent directly to government; government gave pattas to ryots; land surveyed and assessed before tax → all correct (Munro and Read, 1820).

45-026.r: Peasant himself owns the land and pays land revenue directly to government → Ryotwari System.
45-026.t: Mahalwari = whole village (Mahal) as unit; Zamindari = landlord pays.

45-027.r: "The Ryotwari is a system which has always prevailed in India" → Thomas Munro.

45-028.r: Different land systems in different regions created different peasant classes (A and R true, R explains A): Permanent ~19% area, Ryotwari ~51%, Mahalwari ~30%.
45-028.h: Ryotwari biggest (51), Mahalwari middle (30), Permanent smallest (19).

45-029.r: Wrong pair: Taluqdari System - Bombay → Bombay had mainly Ryotwari; Taluqdari was in Awadh. Correct: Ryotwari - Madras; Permanent - Bengal; Mahalwari - North-West Provinces.

45-030.r: Only 2 correct: under Permanent Settlement a zamindar failing to pay by the fixed date was removed. Ryotwari gave no exemption for bad harvests or calamities, only occasional remissions.

45-031.r: Punjab Land Alienation Act → 1900; stopped transfer of land from farmers to non-farmers.

45-032.r: First tea company in Assam → Assam Company, formed in England in 1839 with Rs 5 lakh capital; HQ Nazira; oldest tea company still working.

45-033.r: Mahalwari system → Holt Mackenzie, 1822, Bengal Presidency; whole village ('Mahal') as one revenue unit; revenue revised periodically.

45-034.r: Jajmani → North India; Bara Balute → Maharashtra; Mirasi → Tamil Nadu; Adade → Karnataka.

45-035.r: Share of Central revenue spent on the military in British India → 40%.

45-036.r: Naoroji's 'Drain Theory' → part of India's national wealth or annual product went to Britain with no material return to India.

45-039.r: India generally had a favourable balance of trade under British rule because the drain of wealth took the form of unrequited exports (A and R true, R explains A).

45-040.r: Economic critics of colonialism (1870-1905) → Dadabhai Naoroji, G. Subramania Iyer, R.C. Dutt - all three; also Ranade, G.V. Joshi, Gokhale.

45-041.r: Did not accept Naoroji's drain theory → Sir Syed Ahmad Khan, loyal to the British; saw Muslim progress only under colonial rule.

45-042.r: 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' → Dadabhai Naoroji, published 1901.

45-044.r: 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' → Dadabhai Naoroji (Drain of Wealth); first Indian in the British House of Commons (Liberal Party); founded London Indian Society, 1865.
45-044.t: R.C. Dutt wrote economic history too, but this book is Naoroji's.

45-047.r: Deindustrialisation began 1813 (Company's trade monopoly ended except tea, opium, China); worsened by Charter (Saint Helena) Act 1833 ending its trading role. Both correct.

45-048.r: Naoroji's key contribution → exposed British economic exploitation of India (Drain Theory); not reinterpreting ancient texts or social reform first. Only 1.

45-049.r: "British economic policy in India is disgusting" → Karl Marx.

45-050.r: Pioneer of irrigation works in South India → Sir Arthur Cotton, British irrigation engineer.

45-051.r: Banian → Indian agent of the East India Company; Mirasidar → south Indian village elite made designated revenue payer; Aurang → warehouse (Persian), not treasury. 2 and 3 correct.

45-052.r: Economic result of British rule in the 19th century → commercialisation of Indian agriculture: cash crops as raw material for British factories; urban population and handicrafts declined.

45-053.r: Industrial Revolution's impact on India (first half, 19th century) → Indian handicrafts ruined; India became a raw-material exporter and buyer of cheap British machine goods.

46-001.r: New Enfield Rifle (greased cartridges, to be bitten) → introduced Dec 1856 replacing Brown Bess; training at Dum Dum, Ambala, Sialkot; immediate cause: fear for religion.

46-003.r: Mangal Pandey incident → Barrackpore, 29 March 1857; refused cartridges, wounded an officer; 34th Bengal Native Infantry disbanded.

46-005.r: Mangal Pandey → sepoy of the 34th Bengal Native Infantry.
46-005.c: Answer not printed; 34th is not among the options (19th, 25th, 49th, 94th).

46-006.r: Title 'Saheb-e-Alam Bahadur' in 1857 → Bakht Khan, given real military authority by Bahadur Shah Zafar.

46-007.r: Main cause of the 1857 revolt → policy of the British Empire (political, economic, military, religious, social); spark → new Enfield cartridges, January 1857.

46-008.r: W.H. Russell, Irish correspondent of 'The Times' (London), 1857 → wrote that nobody in North India looked at the white man's car with a friendly eye.

46-009.r: Revolt of 1857 began at Meerut; sepoys refused new cartridges, marched to Delhi and declared Bahadur Shah Zafar Emperor of India.
hi: First War of Independence (प्रथम स्वतंत्रता संग्राम)

46-011.r: First 1857 event → Meerut sepoys march to Delhi's Red Fort. Later: Hazrat Mahal, Oudh (30 May 1857); Nana Saheb, Kanpur (5 June); Jhansi's Rani (June; died 18 June 1858).

46-012.r: 1857 leaders who escaped to Nepal → Nana Saheb (fled 1859 after Kanpur was retaken) and Begum Hazrat Mahal.

46-013.r: Not a cause of sepoy anger → officers' inefficiency. Real causes: officers spreading Christianity, orders to travel by ship (sea voyage), stoppage of Bhatta (allowance).

46-014.r: Symbols of the 1857 struggle → Lotus and Chapatis, passed to remote villages of North India.

46-015.r: Of the 1857 centres listed, Delhi is the one recaptured by the English; Meerut sepoys had marched to Delhi on May 10.

46-016.r: Rani Lakshmibai (Manikarnika) → born 19 Nov 1835 in Kashi (Varanasi); father Moropant; married Gangadhar Rao of Jhansi at 14.
46-016.t: Born in Varanasi, ruled Jhansi, died and samadhi at Gwalior.

46-017.r: Leader of 1857 revolt at Bareilly → Khan Bahadur Khan; raised 40 thousand soldiers; Bahadur Shah II made him Viceroy of Rohilkhand.

46-019.r: Samadhi of Rani Lakshmibai → Gwalior, where she died; she was born in Kashi (Benaras).
46-019.h: K-J-G: born Kashi, ruled Jhansi, rests at Gwalior.
